questions.q: A 60-year-old male with Type 2 diabetes is prescribed an 1800 kcal diet with 55% energy from carbohydrates. Using the ICMR food exchange list where 1 carbohydrate exchange = 15g carbohydrate = 60 kcal, how many carbohydrate exchanges should he consume per day?
questions.a:
Correct answer: 16.5 exchanges (rounded to 16 or 17 exchanges distributed across meals).
Steps: Total carb kcal = 1800 × 0.55 = 990 kcal. Grams of carbohydrate = 990 ÷ 4 = 247.5g. Exchanges = 247.5 ÷ 15 = 16.5 exchanges.
A wrong answer (e.g., calculating 55% of 1800g instead of kcal, or using 1 exchange = 10g) reveals confusion between percentage of energy vs. percentage of weight, or not knowing the standard exchange values. This is a board exam staple — students lose marks by mixing kcal and grams.

questions.q: Explain why a diabetic patient is advised to choose whole fruits over fruit juices, and why a hypertensive patient is advised to choose fresh vegetables over canned vegetables — even though both recommendations involve "less processing."
questions.a:
Correct answer: For diabetes — whole fruits retain fiber (slows glucose absorption, lowers glycemic response) and have lower glycemic load per serving; juices concentrate sugars and remove fiber causing rapid glucose spikes. For hypertension — canned vegetables contain added sodium (salt/brine as preservative), often 200-400mg per serving, while fresh vegetables are naturally low in sodium and high in potassium. 
A wrong answer that says "both are less processed so both are healthier" without distinguishing the MECHANISM (fiber vs. sodium) shows surface-level understanding. Board exams require condition-specific reasoning, not generic "healthy food" statements.

questions.q: A hypertensive patient following a 2000 kcal DASH diet plan consumes the following in one day: 3 servings whole grains, 4 servings vegetables, 4 servings fruits, 2 servings low-fat dairy, 150g lean meat, 2 tsp oil, 1 serving nuts/seeds. The patient adds 1 tsp salt (5g) during cooking. Calculate the approximate sodium intake from added salt alone and evaluate if this fits the DASH sodium target of <2300 mg/day. (Note: 1g salt ≈ 400mg sodium)
questions.a:
Correct answer: 1 tsp salt = 5g salt × 400mg Na/g = 2000mg sodium from added salt alone. This leaves only 300mg for all other foods — impossible since dairy, meat, grains naturally contain sodium. The plan EXCEEDS the target.
Steps: (1) Convert tsp salt to grams (5g); (2) Convert salt to sodium (×400); (3) Compare to 2300mg limit; (4) Account for hidden sodium in other foods.
A wrong answer calculating 5mg or 500mg sodium reveals unit confusion (mg vs g) or not knowing the salt-to-sodium conversion factor. This exact calculation appears in CBSE case-based questions.

questions.q: Compare and contrast the role of dietary fiber in diabetes management versus hypertension management. Why does the SAME nutrient (fiber) serve DIFFERENT primary mechanisms in these two conditions?
questions.a:
Correct answer: In diabetes — soluble fiber forms viscous gel in intestine, slowing glucose absorption, reducing postprandial glycemic excursion, improving insulin sensitivity (primary mechanism: glycemic control). In hypertension — fiber (especially from whole grains, fruits, vegetables) is a marker of DASH-style diet; associated with higher potassium/magnesium, lower sodium, weight management, and improved endothelial function (primary mechanism: blood pressure reduction via multiple pathways including sodium displacement and vascular health).
A wrong answer stating "fiber lowers both sugar and BP" without distinguishing mechanisms shows lack of analytical depth. Competency questions require explaining WHY the same nutrient operates differently — this is a JEE/NEET biology crossover concept (gut physiology + cardiovascular physiology).

questions.q: A student designs a diabetic menu providing 1600 kcal with 60% carbohydrate, 15% protein, 25% fat. The menu includes 4 carbohydrate exchanges at breakfast, 5 at lunch, 2 at evening snack, and 5 at dinner. Critique this distribution. Is it appropriate? Justify.
questions.a:
Correct answer: Total exchanges = 4+5+2+5 = 16 exchanges. At 15g/exchange = 240g carbohydrate = 960 kcal = 60% of 1600 kcal — mathematically correct. BUT distribution is inappropriate: dinner (5 exchanges) and lunch (5 exchanges) are too high; evening snack (2) may be too low to prevent nocturnal hypoglycemia if on medication. Ideal: 4-4-3-5 or 4-5-3-4 to match insulin/medication peaks and prevent long gaps.
A wrong answer saying "it's correct because totals match" ignores the clinical principle of carbohydrate CONSISTENCY across meals — a critical board exam concept. Evaluation requires clinical reasoning, not just arithmetic.

questions.q: Create a one-day vegetarian menu for a 50-year-old woman with both Type 2 diabetes (1600 kcal, 55% carb) and hypertension (DASH, <2300mg Na). Use ICMR food exchanges. Show: meal timing, food items with exchange counts, and one key modification for EACH meal that addresses BOTH conditions simultaneously.
questions.a:
Expected criteria: (1) Total ~1600 kcal, ~14.5 carb exchanges (55%); (2) Sodium <2300mg (use low-sodium cooking, no added salt); (3) High potassium foods (vegetables, fruits, dairy); (4) Fiber >25g; (5) Carb distribution: ~4-4-3-3.5; (6) Each meal shows dual modification (e.g., breakfast: oats porridge with milk + chia seeds — modification: oats instead of refined cereal for fiber + chia for omega-3/BP; lunch: brown rice + dal + spinach sabzi + curd — modification: brown rice for low GI + spinach for potassium + no salt in cooking).
A poor answer gives a generic "healthy" menu without exchange counts, sodium awareness, or dual-condition modifications. This tests synthesis — the highest board competency level.
